That is the oldest prediction machine there is: turn observations into equations, solve, predict beyond them . Long before gradient descent, this is how curves were fit — and in this chapter you rebuild the whole machine, then push it to its breaking point (data that no curve passes through) and invent least squares . Quick Check: Cosine Similarity Quick Check: Two vectors have a cosine similarity of 0. What does this tell you about their relationship? A. They are identical B. They point in exactly opposite directions C. They are perpendicular (at 90 degrees) — knowing one tells you nothing about the other D. One of the vectors is all zeros Answer: C. A cosine similarity of 0 means the vectors are perpendicular — they share no component in each other's direction. Identical vectors give 1.0, opposite vectors give -1.0, and a zero vector is undefined (you cannot divide by zero length).

Through points 1 and 3: slope 4, intercept 4 — but input 2 predicts 12, not 11. No line passes through all three points. Real measurements are noisy; perfect solving just broke. New plan: accept an imperfect line, but pick the one that is least wrong . But how do you measure how wrong a line is? You'll figure that out in the next exercise.

Quick Check: Why Square the Errors? Quick Check: In the least squares method, you minimize the sum of squared errors. Why not just minimize the sum of raw errors (without squaring)? A. Squaring makes the computation faster B. Raw errors can be positive or negative — a prediction 10 too high and one 10 too low would cancel out, giving a total error of 0 even though both predictions are wrong C. Python cannot handle negative numbers in sums D. Squaring is needed because the data might contain negative values Answer: B. Positive and negative errors cancel each other out. Squaring makes every error positive before you add them up. (Taking absolute values would also work, but squaring is smoother — its derivative is a clean formula, which matters when you want to find the minimum.)

What Does a *Random* Matrix Do? Rotation matrices are special. What happens with an arbitrary 2x2 matrix? Build one from random numbers, apply it to the kite with , and plot the result (reuse the plotting code above). Run it several times. Observe, then answer: straight edges stay straight, and parallel edges stay parallel — but lengths and angles change: the kite gets stretched, squashed, sheared, maybe flipped. Every 2x2 matrix is some such linear transformation , and rotations are exactly the ones that preserve all lengths. (When a neural network multiplies data by a learned weight matrix, this stretching and squashing of space is literally what it's doing.)

What you just derived is Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), the same closed-form answer computes. So why does the next chapter exist? Two cracks in the ancient method: solving grows like [math] (your Part 2 estimate), and the derive-and-set-to-zero trick needs a formula for the derivative — which complicated models do not offer. Gradient Descent fixes both by walking toward the minimum instead of jumping to it.
